lesson_title: Why the Apples Grow Halfway Up the Mountain
hook_text: Farmers plant fruit halfway up the slope — never at the bottom. One cold bathtub explains it.
clip_script: And the valley floor? The floor is the bathtub. Cold air streams in off both walls like water down the sides of the tub, and by the small hours the tub has filled: a deep, still pool of the coldest air in the whole landscape lying on the floor, with warmer air resting on its surface. Cold at the bottom, warmer above — upside down from the usual. That upside-down layering is the temperature inversion. And the warm layer floating just above the cold pool has a name every fruit farmer whispers with respect: the thermal belt — the snug shelf partway up the slope that stays warm all night, sitting above the cold bath like the rim of the tub above the waterline.
visual_style: Cross-section animation of a valley at night: blue cold air trickling down both walls and pooling on the floor, a glowing orange band appearing at mid-slope, then a drone shot of real orchards striping that exact height at dawn with frost white on the floor below.
mood: Quiet nature-documentary wonder with a satisfying aha.
pacing: Slow pour of the cold air, glow reveal of the thermal belt, snap match-cut to the real orchards.
